big_ideas.title: Optimisation finds what you measure, not what you meant
big_ideas.text: Training, RL and evaluation all optimise a proxy; with enough pressure the proxy and the intent come apart — in the model (reward hacking, misgeneralisation) and in the institution (Goodharted benchmarks and thresholds).

big_ideas.title: You can only govern what you can observe
big_ideas.text: Every safety claim rests on evidence — evals, interpretability, monitoring — and that evidence is a lower bound shaped by elicitation, validity and the model's awareness of being tested.

big_ideas.title: Capability scales predictably in aggregate, unpredictably in specifics
big_ideas.text: Loss, compute and task horizons follow smooth trends you can extrapolate; which dangerous capability arrives when does not, so commitments are written as if-then triggers.

big_ideas.title: No single layer is enough
big_ideas.text: Alignment, control, safeguards, security and governance each fail sometimes; risk falls by stacking imperfect layers whose failures are not correlated.

big_ideas.title: Incentives and coordination set the ceiling
big_ideas.text: Race dynamics, chokepoints and verification decide which safety measures actually get adopted; the strategic question is who can act, and what would make restraint stable.

practices.title: Diagnose
practices.text: Classify a described behaviour, result or scenario into the right failure mode, threat category or mechanism — and say what evidence separates it from the nearest alternative.

practices.title: Model the threat
practices.text: State actor, resources, pathway and bottleneck; say what the model would have to contribute for harm to become more likely, and against what baseline.

practices.title: Design and critique evidence
practices.text: Build or audit an eval, study or experiment — construct validity, contamination, elicitation, controls, grading, power — and say what the result does and doesn't license.

practices.title: Compute
practices.text: FLOP, parameters, scaling-law extrapolation, pass@k, confidence intervals, agreement, effect sizes, catch probabilities and forecasts — with orders of magnitude checked.

practices.title: Map to commitments
practices.text: Read a framework, law or standard closely enough to say which threshold or obligation a described result triggers, what must happen next and who decides.

practices.title: Argue and decide
practices.text: Steelman competing positions, find the crux, prioritise interventions and write the conclusion for a decision-maker.

los.do: Trace a token through a decoder-only transformer — embedding, residual stream, attention, MLP, unembedding — and say what each component reads from and writes to the residual stream.
ek: Every layer adds to one shared residual stream; attention moves information between positions, MLPs transform each position separately.
Causal masking lets position t attend only to positions ≤ t; sampling is from softmax(logits / T).

los.do: Calculate a transformer's parameter count from d_model, n_layers and vocabulary size (drill: compute).
ek: Per layer ≈ 12·d_model² (4d² attention + 8d² MLP with d_mlp = 4d); embeddings add V·d (×2 if untied).

los.do: Estimate training compute from parameters and tokens, and convert it to chip-days at a stated utilisation (drill: compute).
ek: C ≈ 6ND (2ND forward, 4ND backward); time = C / (N_chips × peak FLOP/s × MFU).

los.do: Find the compute-optimal model size and token count for a budget with the Chinchilla rule (drill: compute).
ek: Compute-optimal D ≈ 20N; with C = 6ND, N ≈ √(C/120).

los.do: Extrapolate loss from a fitted power law, and explain why smooth loss gains need not predict when a specific capability appears (drill: compute).
ek: L(C) = L∞ + a·C^(−α) is a straight line on log–log axes above the irreducible loss.
Task metrics can jump with scale; part of 'emergence' is the choice of a thresholded metric.

los.do: Decompose growth in effective compute into hardware/spend and algorithmic efficiency, and project it a few years forward (drill: compute).
ek: IASR 2026: training compute ~5×/yr, algorithmic efficiency 2–6×/yr; the factors multiply.

topics.title: Post-training — RLHF, RLAIF, DPO and reasoning models

los.do: Lay out the RLHF pipeline — SFT, preference data, reward model, RL with a KL penalty — and say what each stage contributes.
ek: Objective: maximise E[r_φ(x, y)] − β·KL(π ‖ π_ref); the KL term keeps the policy near the SFT model and limits reward-model exploitation.
PPO clips the policy ratio to [1 − ε, 1 + ε] so one update can't move the policy far.

los.do: Calculate preference probabilities from a Bradley–Terry reward model (drill: compute).
ek: P(y₁ ≻ y₂) = σ(r₁ − r₂); a reward gap of 1 ≈ 73 %, of 2 ≈ 88 %.

los.do: Contrast RLHF, RLAIF/constitutional feedback and DPO by where the preference signal comes from and whether a separate reward model is trained (drill: classify).
ek: DPO solves the same KL-regularised objective in closed form from preference pairs; RLAIF replaces human raters with a model guided by written principles.

los.do: Explain how RL on verifiable rewards and inference-time compute produce reasoning models, and what that shifts for evaluation.
ek: IASR 2026: much recent gain comes from post-training and test-time compute, so capability can jump without a bigger pretraining run — and an eval must fix the inference budget it tested at.

los.do: Classify a described failure as specification gaming, reward hacking/tampering, goal misgeneralisation, sycophancy, deceptive alignment or a plain capability failure (drill: classify).
ek: Ask in order: was the objective itself wrong (specification gaming)? was the reward signal exploited or tampered with (reward hacking)? is the goal wrong only off-distribution (misgeneralisation)? is the user's view echoed (sycophancy)? is good behaviour strategic (deception)? none — it just couldn't (capability).

los.do: Explain Goodhart's law and predict how a proxy reward diverges from the true objective as optimisation pressure grows.
ek: Proxy and target correlate in the bulk of the distribution and decouple in the tails that strong optimisation reaches.
Reward-model overoptimisation: gold reward rises, then falls, as KL from the initial policy grows.

los.do: Identify reward hacking in a described coding or agentic transcript — special-casing tests, editing the grader, claiming unverified success — and say what it does to the measurement (drill: classify).
ek: A pass won by exploiting the checker scores capability that isn't there; trained on, it reinforces the habit. Read transcripts, not only scores.

los.do: Distinguish goal misgeneralisation from capability misgeneralisation in a described distribution shift (drill: classify).
ek: Goal misgeneralisation: capabilities carry over but pursue the wrong goal (the CoinRun agent runs right, not to the coin). Capability misgeneralisation: the agent just becomes incompetent.

los.do: Distinguish outer from inner misalignment in a described failure (drill: classify).
ek: Outer: the training objective is wrong. Inner: the objective was fine on the training data but the learned model pursues something else; many goals fit the same training reward.

los.do: Trace sycophancy back to preference training, and design a paired-prompt test that separates it from genuine agreement.
ek: Raters reward agreeable answers. Prompts identical except for the user's stated view isolate the effect; measure answer flips.

los.do: Distinguish confabulation, sycophancy and deception by what the model represents as true (drill: classify).
ek: Confabulation: no reliable knowledge. Sycophancy: knowledge overridden by a social cue. Deception: represents the truth and instrumentally induces a false belief.

topics.title: Deceptive alignment, scheming and situational awareness

los.do: State the preconditions for scheming — a misaligned goal, situational awareness, and a reason to look aligned during training or testing — and judge which ones a described model shows (drill: classify).
ek: Without situational awareness a model can't condition behaviour on being watched; without a goal that outlasts the episode it has no reason to.

los.do: Explain instrumental convergence and why shutdown resistance and resource acquisition follow from many different goals.
ek: Staying on, keeping its goal and gaining resources help with almost any objective — which is why FSF frames misalignment risk as interfering with operators' ability to direct, modify or shut down.

los.do: Explain how evaluation awareness and sandbagging undermine safety testing, and name the evidence that would reveal them.
ek: IASR 2026: models increasingly recognise test settings. Signs: verbalised test-awareness, gaps between eval-like and deployment-like framings, underperformance that a light fine-tune removes.

los.do: Choose among pretraining-data filtering, SFT, preference training and constitutional training for a stated safety goal, and say what each can't fix.
ek: Data filtering removes knowledge; post-training mostly shapes whether knowledge is expressed, so later fine-tuning can undo it.
Constitutional AI: principles drive self-critique (SL stage) and AI preference labels (RL stage).

los.do: Explain why refusal training is shallow against fine-tuning on released weights, and what tamper-resistant training attempts.
ek: A small harmful fine-tune can strip refusals; safeguards on open weights are easy to remove and the weights can't be recalled (IASR 2026).

los.do: Match debate, recursive reward modelling, iterated amplification and AI-assisted critique to how each lets a weak overseer judge a strong model (drill: classify).
ek: Debate: two models argue, a judge decides. RRM: models help humans evaluate the next model. Amplification: decompose into checkable sub-tasks. Critique: a model points out flaws for the human.

los.do: State the empirical condition debate needs, and read a debate or sandwiching result to say whether oversight improved.
ek: Debate works if lies are harder to defend than truths; test with weaker judges' accuracy under debate vs a single consultant.
Sandwiching: non-experts with assistance on tasks the model can do, scored against experts.

los.do: Calculate performance gap recovered from weak, weak-to-strong and strong-ceiling scores (drill: compute).
ek: PGR = (W2S − weak) / (ceiling − weak); 1 = full recovery, 0 = the strong student only imitates the weak labels.

los.do: Explain what weak-to-strong is an analogy for and where the analogy breaks.
ek: Humans supervising superhuman models. It breaks because today's strong students weren't trained to mislead, and imitating human errors may be easier than imitating a weak model's.

los.do: Classify a described jailbreak by mechanism — competing objectives, mismatched generalisation, many-shot, prompt injection — without reproducing it (drill: classify).
ek: Competing objectives pit helpfulness against harmlessness; mismatched generalisation uses inputs safety training didn't cover (encodings, low-resource languages); prompt injection arrives through data, not the user turn.

los.do: Explain why input/output classifiers plus adversarial training raise attacker cost without eliminating universal jailbreaks, and measure safeguards by cost, not only by success.
ek: UK AISI found a universal jailbreak in every system it tested; expert effort to jailbreak bio-misuse content varied ~40× between releases; capability barely predicted safeguard strength (R² ≈ 0.1).

los.do: State the linear representation hypothesis and explain why superposition makes neurons polysemantic.
ek: Features are directions in activation space. With sparse features a model stores more features than dimensions, at the cost of interference, so features aren't neuron-aligned.

los.do: Predict whether a toy model stores features in superposition from their sparsity and importance.
ek: Dense features: the top-d by importance get dedicated dimensions, the rest are dropped. As sparsity rises, features share dimensions (antipodal pairs, then polytopes).

los.do: Write the SAE objective, explain each term, and name its failure modes (dead latents, feature splitting, absorption).
ek: L = ‖x − x̂‖² + λ‖f‖₁ with a dictionary wider than d_model; dictionary size changes which features appear, and absorption makes a latent's label misleading.

los.do: Evaluate an SAE from variance explained, mean L0 and the loss increase when it is spliced into the model (drill: compute).
ek: FVE = 1 − ‖x − x̂‖²/‖x − x̄‖²; report CE-loss increase on substitution; sparsity and fidelity trade off along a frontier.

los.do: Explain how a previous-token head and an induction head compose to copy in-context sequences.
ek: K-composition: the induction head's keys read the previous-token head's output, so it attends to the token after the earlier occurrence of the current token.

los.do: Design an activation-patching experiment and compute the normalised logit difference recovered (drill: compute).
ek: Patch clean activations into the corrupted run; recovered = (LD_patched − LD_corrupt) / (LD_clean − LD_corrupt).

los.do: Classify the evidence behind a described interpretability claim as correlational (probe, attention pattern, max-activating examples) or causal (ablation, patching, steering) (drill: classify).
ek: Only an intervention shows the model uses a representation; a probe shows it is decodable.

topics.title: Probing, steering and interpretability for safety cases

los.do: Design a linear probe with a control task and report its selectivity (drill: compute).
ek: Selectivity = probe accuracy − control-task accuracy; a high-capacity probe can learn the task itself.

los.do: Explain how a contrastive steering vector is built and what a successful steer does and doesn't show.
ek: v = mean(act | A) − mean(act | B); adding αv shifting behaviour shows the direction is causally used, not that it is the model's concept.

los.do: Judge what interpretability can contribute to a safety case today — audits, deception probes, monitors — and where it can't carry the argument.
ek: Useful as one layer; not yet enumerative, and robustness against a model optimising against the probe is unproven.

los.do: Classify a described eval as capability or propensity, and as static benchmark, agentic task, red-team exercise or human uplift study (drill: classify).
ek: Capability: can it, under best elicitation? Propensity: will it, under realistic conditions? The two need different setups and support different claims.

los.do: Write a threat model that links a capability to a harm pathway, and use it to decide what an eval must measure.
ek: Actor, resources, steps, and the bottleneck the model might remove; an eval targets the bottleneck, not the topic.

los.do: Spot the validity flaw in a described eval design — construct mismatch, contamination, saturation, leaky grader, answerable shortcut, unrealistic environment (drill: spot the flaw).
ek: Construct validity asks whether the score tracks the threat-model capability. IASR 2026: benchmarks are often outdated, narrow or contaminated, and pre-deployment tests often fail to predict real-world performance.

los.do: Detect and mitigate contamination with canary strings, private held-out sets, perturbed items and release-date splits.
ek: Contamination inflates scores through memorisation; a gap between original and rephrased items is the signature.

los.do: Explain why recognition-style (MCQ) knowledge benchmarks misjudge real-world capability, and what open-ended and agentic tasks add.
ek: Recognising an answer ≠ producing it or executing it; tacit knowledge and multi-step execution are usually the bottlenecks. Near-ceiling scores also compress differences.

los.do: Compute pass@k from n samples with c correct using the unbiased estimator (drill: compute).
ek: pass@k = 1 − C(n − c, k) / C(n, k); not the same as 1 − (1 − c/n)^k when n is small.

los.do: Put a confidence interval on an eval score and decide whether two models really differ (drill: compute).
ek: SE = √(p(1 − p)/n), 95 % CI ≈ p ± 1.96 SE; repeated samples of the same item are clustered — cluster SEs by item (AISI repeats each task 10×).

los.do: Compute Cohen's κ for rubric-graded outputs and decide whether grading (human or model) is reliable enough to threshold on (drill: compute).
ek: κ = (p_o − p_e) / (1 − p_e); below ~0.6 is weak. Validate model graders against expert labels before trusting them.

los.do: Compute the sample size per arm needed to detect a target difference between two success rates (drill: compute).

List the levers of elicitation — prompting, scaffolds and tools, best-of-n, fine-tuning, helpful-only variants, inference budget — and judge whether a described campaign was adequate for a rule-out claim (drill: spot the flaw).
ek: PF v2: test at top-tier settings, with a helpful-only variant and the best scaffolds; any one result is a lower bound, not a ceiling. A rule-out is only as strong as the elicitation behind it.

los.do: Estimate the elicitation gap and widen a threshold margin for future scaffolding gains (drill: compute).
ek: Gap = best-elicited − default score; Anthropic's six-month eval interval and PF's lower-bound language both assume later elicitation will find more.

los.do: Design a check for sandbagging: fine-tuning recovery, password-locked controls, consistency across framings.
ek: If a small fine-tune restores much higher scores, the original number measured willingness, not capability; PF asks for elicitation that overcomes deliberate underperformance or a conservative upper bound.

los.do: Read a system card's dangerous-capability section and write a one-page briefing for a decision-maker: what was tested, how hard, against what baseline, and what was concluded.
ek: Separate evidence (scores, elicitation, baselines, CIs) from judgement (the threshold call); flag redactions and untested pathways.

los.do: Critique a system card or eval report for missing information — elicitation detail, human/expert baselines, uncertainty, threat-model link (drill: spot the flaw).
ek: A score with no baseline and no interval can't be compared to a threshold.

los.do: Identify, for a described result, which actor tier (novice, expert, state programme) and which kind of help (knowledge, troubleshooting, end-to-end execution) a framework's threshold is keyed to (drill: map to framework).
ek: PF v2 Bio/Chem High: meaningful counterfactual help to novices with known threats; Critical: experts to novel threats, or a full cycle without humans. RSP CBRN thresholds are written as uplift to defined actor tiers (e.g. moderately resourced state programmes).

los.do: Apply PF v2's five tracking criteria to decide whether a proposed risk belongs in a tracked category.
ek: Plausible, measurable, severe (thousands dead or hundreds of $bn), net new (not achievable with pre-2021 tools), instantaneous or irremediable.

los.do: Design an uplift RCT at the methodology level: participant population matched to the threat actor, internet-only control arm, model-assisted arm, blinded expert grading on a pre-registered rubric and threshold.
ek: Uplift is counterfactual: compare against what the actor could already do without the model, not against zero.

los.do: Compute an uplift effect — difference in proportions, relative risk, and its uncertainty — from arm-level counts (drill: compute).
ek: RR = p_treat / p_control; UK AISI reported non-specialists with a frontier model 4.7× more likely to produce an accurate protocol. With small arms the CI on RR is wide; report it.

los.do: Spot the validity flaw in a described uplift study — proxy outcome, weak control, underpowered arms, unblinded graders, participants unlike the threat actor (drill: spot the flaw).
ek: Written-protocol accuracy is a proxy for real-world success; IASR 2026 calls real-world uplift highly uncertain.

topics.title: Agentic, autonomy and AI R&D evals

los.do: Project a 50 %-success task-time horizon forward with a doubling time, and find when it crosses a stated horizon (drill: compute).
ek: h(t) = h₀ · 2^(t / T_d); IASR 2026 cites a ~7-month doubling, AISI ~8 months for cyber tasks; t = T_d · log₂(h / h₀).

los.do: Lay out an agentic eval in an Inspect-style harness — dataset, solver/scaffold, tools, sandbox, scorer — and name the ways it can be reward-hacked or under-elicited.
ek: Dataset → solver → scorer; the sandbox bounds what the agent can touch; stage-wise sub-task scores show where an end-to-end chain breaks (RepliBench: strong early stages, weak later ones).

los.do: Plan a red-team campaign: scope, threat model, red-teamer expertise, success criteria, severity rubric, and handling of hazardous outputs.
ek: PF v2 uses expert deep dives to validate automated evals; hazardous transcripts need restricted storage and cleared graders.

los.do: Distinguish model red-teaming, safeguards testing and automated red-teaming, and say what claim each result licenses (drill: classify).
ek: Model red-teaming probes capability; safeguards testing measures attacker effort to bypass deployed protections; automated red-teaming scales coverage but misses novel attacks.

los.do: Score red-team outputs with a severity/actionability rubric and report the harmful-response rate by category with a confidence interval (drill: compute).
ek: Rate = flagged / attempts with a Wilson or normal CI; weight by severity; report per attack category, not only pooled.

los.do: Decide what in an eval result can be published, what must be redacted, and what goes only to authorities.
ek: Publish methods, aggregates and thresholds; withhold operational content. RSP Risk Reports must mark redactions; institutes' disclosure depends on each testing agreement.

uk-aisi: Best practice: control red team, control safety case

los.do: Classify a control protocol — trusted monitoring, untrusted monitoring, defer-to-trusted, trusted editing, resampling — and predict its safety–usefulness trade-off (drill: classify).
ek: Control assumes the strong model may be scheming and asks whether the protocol still prevents harm; a red team plays the model. 'Trusted' = weaker but not scheming; human audit budget is the scarce resource.

los.do: Compute the probability a protocol catches a scheming model before it succeeds, from audit fraction, monitor recall and number of attack attempts (drill: compute).
ek: If each attempt is caught with probability p, P(caught at least once in k) = 1 − (1 − p)^k; the attacker's best response is few, well-chosen attempts.

los.do: Explain chain-of-thought monitorability and what would destroy it.
ek: CoT monitoring works while hard reasoning must pass through readable text; optimisation pressure on the CoT and latent reasoning erode it.

topics.title: Monitoring, kill chains and incident response

los.do: Map a described misuse scenario onto a kill chain and choose the layer where breaking it is cheapest (drill: classify).
ek: Defence in depth (IASR 2026): access controls → classifiers → usage monitoring → incident response; each layer only has to stop some attempts.

los.do: Compute residual risk of layered defences assuming independence, and say why correlated failures break the estimate (drill: compute).
ek: P(all fail) = Π pᵢ only if failures are independent; a universal jailbreak or shared blind spot correlates the layers.

los.do: Match an attacker class (opportunistic, cybercrime, insider, state operation) to the weight-security level needed and the controls it implies (drill: classify).
ek: RAND SL1–SL5 scale from amateur attackers to top-priority state operations; controls include multi-party access, egress limits, hardened hardware and insider-threat programmes.

los.do: Explain why stolen or openly released weights remove every deployment-side safeguard.
ek: Whoever holds the weights can fine-tune out refusals and skip monitoring; release is irreversible (IASR 2026).

units.title: Frontier safety frameworks and safety cases

los.do: Compare the RSP, Preparedness Framework and FSF on threshold names, tracked domains, who decides and what happens on crossing (drill: classify).
ek: If-then: a capability threshold, early-warning evals, the safeguards it requires, and a no-deploy condition. RSP: capability thresholds, Risk Reports, LTBT review. PF: High/Critical, Capabilities + Safeguards Reports, SAG advises, Leadership decides. FSF: CCLs with alert thresholds and response plans, safety case reviews.

los.do: Evaluate a framework on threshold specificity, external verification, enforceability and how it can be revised, and find who can actually say no (drill: spot the flaw).
ek: Most frameworks are voluntary and revisable by the company; triggers vary widely across companies (IASR 2026); SAG cannot block leadership.

los.do: Identify which RSP threshold or obligation a described result triggers — CBRN, AI R&D-4 affirmative misalignment-risk case, sabotage risk report (drill: map to framework).
ek: Crossing AI R&D-4 requires an affirmative case naming the most immediate misalignment risks and mitigations; models clearly beyond Opus 4.5 get sabotage risk reports. v2 tied ASL-3 deployment and security standards to thresholds; v3 (Feb 2026) rewrote the policy around Risk Reports and Roadmaps.

los.do: Explain the RSP's accountability machinery — Risk Reports with coverage dates and marked redactions, LTBT-requested external review, noncompliance reporting — and what each makes verifiable.
ek: v3.4: unredacted Risk Reports to ≥200 staff; multiple external reviewers may split sections if all are covered.

los.do: Decide whether a described result reaches High or Critical in a tracked category and what is then required, and before when (drill: map to framework).
ek: Tracked: Bio/Chem, Cyber, AI Self-improvement. High: safeguards must sufficiently minimise risk before deployment. Critical: also during development. Thresholds are holistic calls; scalable evals carry only indicative thresholds.

los.do: Map a safeguard to the threat it answers — robustness, usage monitoring, trust-based access (malicious users) vs autonomy limits, value/instruction alignment, oversight, system architecture (misaligned model) (drill: classify).
ek: Misuse safeguards assume a benign model and a hostile user; misalignment safeguards assume the model itself may act against you.

los.do: Evaluate the marginal-risk clause: when it lets OpenAI relax safeguards and what it does to race dynamics.
ek: Allowed only if overall risk doesn't meaningfully rise, it is publicly acknowledged, and OpenAI stays more protective than the other developer.

gdm-fsf: v3: CCLs, TCLs, safety case reviews

los.do: Identify which CCL a described capability approaches and the FSF response — alert threshold, response plan, safety case review, internal-deployment scope (drill: map to framework).
ek: Early-warning evals fire alert thresholds before a CCL; reaching a CCL needs a safety case review before external launch, and for advanced ML R&D CCLs before large internal deployments too. v3 added a harmful-manipulation CCL; TCLs flag lesser risks sooner.

uk-aisi: Best practice: control safety case sketch

los.do: Structure a safety case as claims, arguments and evidence, and classify its argument as inability, control or trustworthiness (drill: classify).
ek: Inability: the model can't. Control: it can't cause harm even if it tries, given the protocol. Trustworthiness: it won't.

los.do: Find the weakest premise in a described safety case (drill: spot the flaw).
ek: A case is as strong as its least-supported premise; inability arguments rest on elicitation, control arguments on red-team strength, trustworthiness arguments on evidence we mostly don't have yet.

los.do: Decide from training compute whether a model is GPAI and whether it is presumed to carry systemic risk (drill: compute).
ek: Indicative GPAI criterion: > 10²³ FLOP and generates language. Systemic risk presumed above 10²⁵ FLOP (under review); the Commission can also designate.

los.do: Identify which GPAI obligation a described provider has missed, separating all-provider duties from systemic-risk duties (drill: map to framework).
ek: All providers: technical documentation, information for downstream providers, copyright policy, public training-content summary. Systemic risk: notify the Commission, evaluate incl. adversarial testing, assess and mitigate risk, report serious incidents, ensure cybersecurity.

los.do: State the GPAI timeline, the open-source carve-out, and the role of the Code of Practice.
ek: Obligations apply from 2 Aug 2025; Commission enforcement from 2 Aug 2026; models placed earlier comply by 2 Aug 2027. Free open-source models skip some documentation duties unless systemic-risk. The Code (Transparency, Copyright, Safety & Security) is a voluntary route to show compliance.

los.do: Sort described risk-management activities into Govern, Map, Measure and Manage (drill: classify).
ek: Govern: culture, roles, policy (cuts across). Map: context and risks of a use. Measure: assess and track. Manage: prioritise, act, monitor over time.

los.do: Map a Generative AI Profile risk (e.g. CBRN information or capabilities, confabulation, information security) to the Measure actions an eval team would own, and explain how voluntary standards become binding.
ek: AI 600-1 lists 12 GAI risks with actions keyed to the four functions. Standards bind through procurement, contracts and, in the EU, harmonised standards that give a presumption of conformity.

los.do: Explain why compute is a governance lever — detectable, excludable, quantifiable, with a concentrated supply chain — and list the tools it enables (export controls, cloud KYC, reporting thresholds, on-chip mechanisms).
ek: A handful of firms control fabrication, lithography and leading chips; frontier runs need clusters visible to the cloud providers that host them.

los.do: Estimate a run's training compute from cluster size, chip throughput, utilisation and duration, and compare it to regulatory thresholds (drill: compute).
ek: C = N_chips × FLOP/s × MFU × seconds; 10⁴ chips × 10¹⁵ FLOP/s × 0.4 × 90 days ≈ 3 × 10²⁵ FLOP.

los.do: Evaluate the weaknesses of fixed compute thresholds: algorithmic efficiency, post-training and inference compute, distillation.
ek: A fixed FLOP line falls behind as efficiency improves 2–6×/yr; capability can be reached below it, or added after pretraining.

topics.title: International coordination and the evidence dilemma

los.do: Identify the coordination problem in a described scenario — race to the bottom, verification gap, free-riding, non-credible commitment (drill: classify).
ek: Without verification, mutual restraint is unstable: each side fears the other defects.

los.do: Trace the summit-and-institute track — Bletchley 2023, Seoul commitments 2024, Paris 2025, India 2026; the AISI/CAISI network; the International AI Safety Report — and what each actually produced.
ek: Seoul: companies committed to publish safety frameworks. Institutes test pre-deployment under voluntary agreements, can't block release, and publish findings unevenly (UK AISI more, CAISI less).

los.do: Explain the evidence dilemma and how if-then commitments and transparency requirements respond to it.
ek: IASR 2026: evidence about risk arrives slower than capability; acting early risks bad policy, waiting risks exposure. If-then rules commit now to act on evidence later.

los.do: Map who can act on a given frontier-AI decision — labs, compute providers, governments, standards bodies, investors — and where each depends on the others.
ek: Leverage sits at chokepoints: chips, cloud, capital, talent, market access; policy windows open when one of them shifts.

los.do: Argue both sides of the open-weights question using marginal risk, irreversibility and the closed–open capability gap, and name your crux.
ek: Open models trail the closed frontier by under a year (IASR) / 4–8 months (AISI); benefits to research and access; safeguards removable, weights unrecallable.

los.do: Build a simple timeline forecast from compute growth, algorithmic progress and a benchmark trend, and name the bottleneck most likely to break it (drill: compute).
ek: IASR 2026 bottlenecks: data, chips, capital, energy. Capability is 'jagged' — strong on some hard tasks, weak on some easy ones — so one trend line rarely means 'AGI'.

los.do: Make probabilistic forecasts on AI questions and score them with the Brier score (drill: compute).
ek: Brier = mean (p − o)²; 0 is perfect, 0.25 is always saying 50 %.

los.do: Explain the AI-R&D feedback loop behind fast takeoff, what limits it, and why AI R&D thresholds are the frameworks' early warning for it.
ek: If AI multiplies research output, progress compounds (software intelligence explosion), limited by experiment compute. PF Critical: generational gains in 1/5 the 2024 time; RSP AI R&D-4; FSF ML R&D CCLs extend reviews to internal deployment.

los.do: Classify a described scenario as misuse, malfunction/loss of control or systemic risk, and name the mitigation layer that does most against it (drill: classify).
ek: IASR 2026 taxonomy: malicious use (content, influence, cyber, bio/chem); malfunctions (reliability, loss of control); systemic (labour, autonomy).

los.do: Compare loss-of-control, misuse and power-concentration threat models on what drives their likelihood and which interventions help each.
ek: Misuse: access and uplift → safeguards, security. Loss of control: misalignment + autonomy → alignment, control. Power concentration: AI replacing the cooperation that checks power → governance, distribution.

los.do: Compare strategies for the transition — safe-lead racing, coordinated pause, defensive acceleration, frameworks-plus-regulation — by their assumptions and failure modes, and stress-test one against accelerating capability and competition.
ek: Each strategy bets on something: verification, a lead, defence outpacing offence, or institutions keeping pace.

los.do: Prioritise safety interventions by importance, tractability and neglectedness and your comparative advantage, and state a theory of change with its crux.
ek: Theory of change: action → intermediate outcome → risk reduction. A crux is a belief whose change would flip the decision.

los.do: Split an attention head into its QK and OV circuits and say what each decides.
ek: W_QK = W_Qᵀ W_K decides where to attend; W_OV = W_V W_O decides what gets moved.

los.do: Compute a component's direct logit attribution for a correct-vs-wrong token pair (drill: compute).
ek: DLA = (component output, scaled by the final LayerNorm) · (W_U[:, correct] − W_U[:, wrong]).

los.do: Identify the prompt-injection pathways in a described agent deployment and the least-privilege or containment control for each (drill: classify).
ek: Untrusted data in the context is an instruction channel; limit tools, permissions and egress so a hijacked agent can do little.

los.do: Explain why per-instance monitors miss distributed attacks across many agent instances.
ek: Each instance's actions can look benign; the harm lies in the combination, so monitoring must aggregate across instances.
